newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Dairy Farm sees short-term pain.
newsitem.headline: Dairy Farm sees short-term pain.

text.p: Dairy Farm International Holdings Ltd said the costs of investment in new businesses and repositioning of certain activities, particularly in Australia, meant the group expected lower earnings this year.

Tough market conditions or the need to invest heavily in new or expanding businesses in Australia, Taiwan, China and Britain offset positive performances in Hong Kong, Singapore, Spain and New Zealand, company executives said on Thursday.
"The major challenge is Australia," said Chris Nelson, group chief executive, by telephone.

Dairy Farm, part of the Jardine Matheson Holdings Ltd stable of companies managed from Hong Kong but with primary share listings in London, saw turnover rise nine percent in the six months ended June 30, 1996.
But trading profits slipped 39 percent and earnings per share tumbled 62 percent.
The company warned it expected earnings in 1996 to fall short of those in 1995, but said it intended to maintain the dividend for the year unchanged on last year's level.
"Dairy Farm is meeting the twin challenges of entering new markets in the high-growth Asian economies and of adapting its mature businesses to changing customer environments.
"This inevitably weighs on profits in the near term," company chairman Simon Keswick said in a statement from London.

The infrastructural costs of repositioning its Franklins food concerns in Australia into fresh and perishable products had proved greater than expected, finance director Edouard Ettedgui said in Hong Kong.
Ettedgui said the overall cost of this repositioning would hold back Franklins' profit recovery over the next 18 months to two years.
In Taiwan, competitive pressures led to disappointing performances, Nelson said.
In the face of fierce price competition, the group added 28 Mannings drug stores in Taiwan in the past 18 months, bringing the total to 60.
The four-year-old Nestle SA Dairy Farm ice cream joint venture continued to experience difficult times in Hong Kong where established brands are entrenched.
But its ice cream manufacturing operations in the Chinese cities of Qingdao and Tianjin had gotten underway and, while start-up losses were inevitable, the company was optimistic for the longer term.

On the positive side, Dairy Farm's Hong Kong operations, other than the ice cream joint venture, performed well, with restaurant division Maxims experiencing a 10 percent increase in profit despite a retail slump in the colony.
Its Wellcome supermarket chain and Olivers gourmet shop chain achieved modest profit increases.

However, investment in improving the just-in-time distribution system for its 7-Eleven stores, centred on the Asia Terminals Ltd facility at the Kwai Chung container port, resulted in a lower contribution from the division.
Spanish and New Zealand retailing operations performed well, but Nelson said increasing competition affected its Kwik Save supermarket operations in Britain.
The company said Kwik Save's sales rose eight percent but profit fell 28 percent as a result of the competition.
Kwik Save's business strategy was now being reviewed, the company said but did not elaborate.
